questions.subject: English

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
questions.explanation: Plural subject 'they' takes the plural verb 'are'.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.

options.A: Each of the students have a book.
options.B: Each of the students has a book.
options.C: Each of the students are having a book.
options.D: Each of the students having a book.

questions.explanation: 'Each' is an indefinite pronoun that takes a singular verb. The subject is 'each', not 'students'.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
questions.explanation: 'Everyone' is a singular indefinite pronoun and takes a singular verb 'is'.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Choose the correct sentence (traditional exam pattern).

options.A: Neither of the answers are correct.
options.B: Neither of the answers is correct.
options.C: Neither of the answers were correct.
options.D: Neither of the answers have correct.

questions.explanation: 'Neither' is a singular indefinite pronoun and traditionally takes a singular verb in exam patterns.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
questions.explanation: 'News' is singular in form and takes a singular verb 'is'.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
questions.explanation: 'Mathematics' is a singular subject despite ending in 's' and takes 'is'.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.

options.A: The quality of the products are good.
options.B: The quality of the products is good.
options.C: The quality of the products were good.
options.D: The quality of the products have good.

questions.explanation: The real subject is 'quality' (singular), not 'products'. Intervening phrases do not determine verb agreement.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
questions.explanation: Plural subject 'boys' takes the plural verb 'play'.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is subject-verb agreement?

options.A: The verb must agree with its object in number and person.
options.B: The verb must agree with its subject in number and person.
options.C: The subject must agree with its verb in tense only.
options.D: The adjective must agree with the noun in number.

questions.explanation: Subject-verb agreement means the verb must agree with its subject in number and person.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which indefinite pronouns generally take singular verbs?

options.B: Each, every, everyone, everybody, someone, somebody, anyone, nobody, either, neither

questions.explanation: Each, every, everyone, everybody, someone, somebody, anyone, nobody, either, and neither generally take singular verbs.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Does a phrase beginning with 'along with' change the subject's number?

options.A: Yes, it makes the subject plural.
options.B: No, the verb agrees with the main subject.
options.C: Yes, it makes the subject singular.
options.D: It depends on the tense used.

questions.explanation: No. 'The teacher, along with the students, is present.' The verb agrees with the main subject 'teacher'.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.

options.A: The teacher, along with the students, are present.
options.B: The teacher, along with the students, is present.
options.C: The teacher, along with the students, were present.
options.D: The teacher, along with the students, have present.

questions.explanation: The phrase 'along with the students' does not change the number of the main subject 'teacher', which is singular.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: How does either...or / neither...nor affect agreement?

options.A: The verb always agrees with the first subject.
options.B: The verb generally agrees with the nearer subject.

questions.explanation: The verb generally agrees with the nearer subject: 'Neither the teacher nor the students are ready'; 'Neither the students nor the teacher is ready.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.

options.A: Neither the teacher nor the students is ready.
options.B: Neither the teacher nor the students are ready.
options.C: Neither the teacher nor the students was ready.
options.D: Neither the teacher nor the students has ready.

questions.explanation: With 'neither...nor', the verb agrees with the nearer subject 'students' (plural), so 'are' is correct.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.

options.A: Neither the students nor the teacher are ready.
options.B: Neither the students nor the teacher is ready.
options.C: Neither the students nor the teacher were ready.
options.D: Neither the students nor the teacher have ready.

questions.explanation: With 'neither...nor', the verb agrees with the nearer subject 'teacher' (singular), so 'is' is correct.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which uncountable nouns usually take singular verbs?

options.B: Information, advice, furniture, equipment, luggage, knowledge, scenery

questions.explanation: Information, advice, furniture, equipment, luggage, knowledge, and scenery are uncountable nouns that take singular verbs.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.

options.A: The furniture in these rooms are new.
options.B: The furniture in these rooms is new.
options.C: The furniture in these rooms were new.
options.D: The furniture in these rooms have new.

questions.explanation: 'Furniture' is an uncountable noun and takes a singular verb 'is'.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Can collective nouns take plural verbs?

options.B: Yes, depending on whether the group is viewed as a unit or as individual members.

questions.explanation: Collective nouns can take plural verbs depending on whether the group is viewed as a unit or as individual members. Examination convention and context matter.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
questions.explanation: Simple past is used for a completed action at a definite past time ('yesterday'). The past tense of 'go' is 'went'.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
questions.explanation: 'Know' is a stative verb and is not normally used in continuous forms. Simple present 'know' is correct.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
questions.explanation: With a definite past time ('yesterday'), simple past 'completed' is used, not present perfect.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.

options.A: They have waited since two hours.
options.B: They have waited for two hours.
options.C: They have waited from two hours.
options.D: They have waited at two hours.

questions.explanation: 'For' is used with a duration (two hours). 'Since' is used with a starting point.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
questions.explanation: After 'did/did not', the base form of the verb is used: 'did not go'.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.

options.A: When I reached, he already left.
options.B: When I reached, he had already left.
options.C: When I reached, he has already left.
options.D: When I reached, he was already left.

questions.explanation: Past perfect 'had already left' is used for an action completed before another past action ('reached').

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.

options.A: I will call when he will arrive.
options.B: I will call when he arrives.
options.C: I will call when he arrived.
options.D: I will call when he is arriving.

questions.explanation: In future-time clauses after 'when', 'before', 'after', 'until', and 'as soon as', present simple is used.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.

options.B: She has been living here since 2020.

questions.explanation: Present perfect continuous 'has been living' is used with 'since' for an action continuing from a past starting point.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: When is the simple past used?

options.A: For an action continuing to the present.
options.B: For a completed action at a definite past time.
options.D: For a habitual action in the present.

questions.explanation: Simple past is used for a completed action at a definite past time: yesterday, last week, in 2020.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: When is 'since' used?
questions.explanation: 'Since' is used with a starting point: since Monday, since 2020, since morning.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: When is 'for' used?
questions.explanation: 'For' is used with a duration: for two hours, for three years.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which verb form follows did/did not?
questions.explanation: The base form follows did/did not: did go, did not see (not did went or did not saw).

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which tense is commonly used in future-time clauses after when, before, after, until and as soon as?
questions.explanation: Present simple is used: 'I will call you when he arrives.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which verbs are usually stative in their ordinary meanings?

options.B: Know, believe, understand, belong, own, seem

questions.explanation: Know, believe, understand, belong, own, and seem are stative verbs not normally used in continuous forms in those meanings.

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.

options.B: The sun rises in the east.
options.C: A sun rises in a east.

questions.explanation: 'The' is used with unique objects (the sun) and specific directions (the east).

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
questions.explanation: 'The' is used with superlatives: 'the best player'.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.

options.A: The gold is a precious metal.
options.D: An gold is a precious metal.

questions.explanation: Zero article is used with uncountable nouns used generally: 'Gold is a precious metal.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: How do 'a' and 'an' differ?

options.A: Use 'a' before a vowel letter and 'an' before a consonant letter.
options.B: Use 'a' before a consonant sound and 'an' before a vowel sound.
options.C: Use 'a' for plural nouns and 'an' for singular nouns.
options.D: Use 'a' for countable nouns and 'an' for uncountable nouns.

questions.explanation: Use 'a' before a consonant sound and 'an' before a vowel sound; the sound, not the letter, determines the choice.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: When is 'the' used?

options.B: For specific or identified nouns, many unique objects, and with superlatives.

questions.explanation: 'The' is used for specific or identified nouns and many unique objects; also with superlatives.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: When is the zero article used?

options.B: Often with plural or uncountable nouns used generally.

questions.explanation: Zero article is often used with plural or uncountable nouns used generally: 'Books are useful'; 'Water is essential.'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.

options.B: He is suffering from a fever.

questions.explanation: The correct preposition is 'suffer from'.

questions.question: Choose the correct fixed combination: He depends ___ his parents.

questions.explanation: The correct fixed combination is 'listen to music'.

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
questions.explanation: The correct fixed combination is 'insist on'.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.

options.A: I congratulated him for his success.
options.B: I congratulated him on his success.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
questions.explanation: Subject pronouns (I) are used for the subject; 'Ravi and I' is the conventional order.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.

options.A: Between you and I, this is wrong.
options.B: Between you and me, this is wrong.
options.C: Between you and he, this is wrong.
options.D: Between you and they, this is wrong.

questions.explanation: After a preposition, an object pronoun is used: 'between you and me'.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
questions.explanation: The object pronoun 'him' is used as the object of the verb 'punished'.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the difference between subject and object pronouns?

options.A: Subject forms: me, him, her, us, them; Object forms: I, he, she, we, they
options.B: Subject forms: I, he, she, we, they; Object forms: me, him, her, us, them
options.D: Subject forms are used after prepositions.

questions.explanation: Subject forms: I, he, she, we, they. Object forms: me, him, her, us, them.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Is singular 'they' grammatically acceptable?

options.B: Yes, in modern standard English for an unknown or unspecified person.

questions.explanation: Singular 'they' is acceptable in modern standard English for an unknown or unspecified person. Some older exam keys may follow traditional 'his or her' usage.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
questions.explanation: Adverbs modify verbs. 'Beautifully' is the adverb form modifying 'sings'.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
questions.explanation: Adverbs modify verbs. 'Quickly' is the adverb form modifying 'runs'.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.

options.A: She is the most tallest girl.
options.C: She is the more tallest girl.

questions.explanation: 'Tallest' is already superlative; 'most tallest' is redundant.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
questions.explanation: 'Enough' follows the adjective it modifies: 'strong enough'.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Choose the correct sentence (meaning: feel unhappy).
questions.explanation: After linking verbs such as feel, an adjective is often required when describing the subject. 'Feel bad' means feel unhappy.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the rule regarding adjectives and adverbs?

options.A: Adjectives modify verbs; adverbs modify nouns.
options.B: Adjectives modify nouns and linking-verb complements; adverbs commonly modify verbs, adjectives or other adverbs.
options.C: Both adjectives and adverbs modify nouns only.

questions.explanation: Adjectives modify nouns and linking-verb complements; adverbs commonly modify verbs, adjectives or other adverbs.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.

options.A: Although he was poor, but he was honest.
options.B: Although he was poor, he was honest.
options.C: Although he was poor, and he was honest.
options.D: Although he was poor, so he was honest.

questions.explanation: 'Although' and 'but' should not be used together. Use one or the other.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.

options.A: Unless you do not work, you will fail.
options.B: Unless you work, you will fail.
options.C: Unless you will work, you will fail.
options.D: Unless you work not, you will fail.

questions.explanation: 'Unless' already means 'if not', so 'do not' is not used with it.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
questions.explanation: The correct pairing is 'neither...nor'.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.

options.A: No sooner he arrived than it rained.
options.B: No sooner had he arrived than it rained.
options.C: No sooner he had arrived than it rained.
options.D: No sooner did he arrived than it rained.

questions.explanation: Inversion is required after 'no sooner': 'No sooner had he arrived than...'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.

options.A: Hardly had he reached than the train left.
options.B: Hardly had he reached when the train left.
options.C: Hardly he had reached when the train left.
options.D: Hardly had he reached then the train left.

questions.explanation: The correct pairing is 'hardly/scarcely...when'.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which of the following is a correct conjunction pairing?
questions.explanation: Correct pairings: either...or; neither...nor; both...and; not only...but also; no sooner...than; hardly/scarcely...when.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
questions.explanation: Make + object takes a bare infinitive: 'made me laugh'.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.

options.A: I look forward to meet you.
options.B: I look forward to meeting you.
options.C: I look forward to met you.

questions.explanation: 'To' in 'look forward to' is a preposition, so a gerund follows: 'meeting'.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
questions.explanation: Verbs like enjoy, avoid, finish, and consider take a gerund (-ing form).

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.

options.B: He suggested that I should go.

questions.explanation: 'Suggest' does not take an object + infinitive. Correct patterns: 'suggested that I should go' or 'suggested going'.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
questions.explanation: 'Enjoy' takes a gerund: 'enjoy reading'.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
questions.explanation: 'Let' takes a bare infinitive: 'Let him speak.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.

options.A: She is used to wake up early.
options.B: She is used to waking up early.
options.C: She is used to woke up early.
options.D: She used to waking up early.

questions.explanation: 'Be used to' takes a noun/gerund meaning 'accustomed to'. 'Used to + base verb' expresses a past habit.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
questions.explanation: Present perfect uses the past participle: 'has gone'.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which form follows make + object in the active voice?
questions.explanation: Bare infinitive: 'They made him apologise.' In the passive, 'to' is used: 'He was made to apologise.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which form follows enjoy, avoid, finish and consider?
questions.explanation: A gerund (-ing form) follows: enjoy reading, avoid arguing, finish writing, consider moving.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the difference between 'used to' and 'be used to'?

options.B: 'Used to + base verb' expresses a past habit; 'be used to + noun/gerund' means accustomed to something.
options.C: 'Used to' is for the present; 'be used to' is for the past.
options.D: 'Used to' takes a gerund; 'be used to' takes a base verb.

questions.explanation: 'Used to + base verb' expresses a past habit; 'be used to + noun/gerund' means accustomed to something.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is a sentence fragment?

options.A: Two independent clauses joined without correct punctuation.
options.B: An incomplete group of words incorrectly presented as a complete sentence.
options.C: A modifier placed so that it appears to describe the wrong word.
options.D: Using unlike grammatical forms in a series.

questions.explanation: A sentence fragment is an incomplete group of words incorrectly presented as a complete sentence. Example: 'Because he was late.' Correct: 'Because he was late, he missed the bus.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is a run-on sentence?

options.A: A sentence that is too long.
options.B: Two or more independent clauses joined without correct punctuation or conjunction.
options.C: A sentence with a dangling modifier.

questions.explanation: A run-on sentence joins two or more independent clauses without correct punctuation or conjunction. Correct with a full stop, semicolon or comma plus coordinator.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is a comma splice?

options.A: Two independent clauses joined only by a comma.
options.B: A comma used incorrectly in a list.
options.C: A missing comma after an introductory phrase.
options.D: A comma used with a conjunction.

questions.explanation: A comma splice joins two independent clauses only by a comma: 'It was late, we went home.' Correct: 'It was late, so we went home.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is a misplaced modifier?

options.A: A modifier with no clear word to modify.
options.B: A modifier placed so that it appears to describe the wrong word.
options.C: Using unlike grammatical forms in a series.

questions.explanation: A misplaced modifier is placed so that it appears to describe the wrong word. Example: 'She almost drove her children to school every day' may mean she nearly drove but did not. Place 'almost' beside the intended element.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is a dangling modifier?

options.A: A modifier that is too far from the word it modifies.
options.B: A modifying phrase that has no clear or logical word to modify.
options.C: A modifier that modifies two words at once.

questions.explanation: A dangling modifier has no clear or logical word to modify. Incorrect: 'Walking down the road, the trees looked beautiful.' Correct: 'Walking down the road, I thought the trees looked beautiful.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is faulty parallelism?

options.A: Using unlike grammatical forms in a series or paired construction.
options.C: Two independent clauses joined by a comma.
options.D: A modifier with no clear word to modify.

questions.explanation: Faulty parallelism uses unlike grammatical forms in a series or paired construction. Incorrect: 'She likes reading, to swim and dancing.' Correct: 'She likes reading, swimming and dancing.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is a faulty comparison?

options.A: Comparing unlike things or omitting the comparison group.
options.B: Using unlike grammatical forms in a series.
options.C: Two independent clauses joined by a comma.
options.D: A modifier with no clear word to modify.

questions.explanation: A faulty comparison compares unlike things or omits the comparison group. Incorrect: 'The climate of Bengaluru is better than Delhi.' Correct: 'The climate of Bengaluru is better than that of Delhi.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is an ambiguous sentence?

options.A: A sentence with a grammatical error.
options.B: A sentence that can reasonably have more than one meaning because of unclear wording or structure.
options.C: A sentence with a missing word.

questions.explanation: An ambiguous sentence can reasonably have more than one meaning because of unclear wording or structure.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is a split or unclear reference?

options.A: A pronoun or demonstrative that has no clear antecedent.
options.B: A verb that does not agree with its subject.
options.C: A modifier placed too far from the word it modifies.
options.D: A sentence with two independent clauses.

questions.explanation: A split or unclear reference occurs when a pronoun or demonstrative has no clear antecedent. Replace it with a clear noun or restructure the sentence.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is a subject-verb split error?

options.A: The verb is placed too far from the subject.
options.B: The writer is misled by words between subject and verb.
options.C: The subject is missing from the sentence.
options.D: The verb is in the wrong tense.

questions.explanation: The writer is misled by words between subject and verb. Find the actual subject: 'The list of items is on the desk.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is a double negative?

options.A: Two negative forms used where standard English requires one.
options.B: Two negative sentences in a row.
options.C: A negative sentence with a positive meaning.
options.D: A sentence with no negative words.

questions.explanation: A double negative uses two negative forms where standard English requires one: 'I don't know nothing.' Correct: 'I don't know anything.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is an illogical sequence?

options.A: A sentence with a grammatical error.
options.B: A sentence with a spelling mistake.
options.C: A sentence whose order of events or ideas is inconsistent with the intended chronology or logic.
options.D: A sentence with two independent clauses.

questions.explanation: An illogical sequence is a sentence whose order of events or ideas is inconsistent with the intended chronology or logic.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Identify the error type: 'Because it was raining. We stayed home.'
questions.explanation: 'Because it was raining.' is a fragment (incomplete sentence). Correct: 'Because it was raining, we stayed home.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Identify the error type: 'I was tired, I went to bed.'
questions.explanation: Two independent clauses joined only by a comma form a comma splice. Correct: 'I was tired, so I went to bed.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Identify the error type: 'Walking to school, the rain started.'
questions.explanation: The modifying phrase 'Walking to school' has no logical subject (the rain wasn't walking). Correct: 'While I was walking to school, it started raining.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Identify the error type: 'She likes singing, to dance and reading.'
questions.explanation: The series mixes gerunds ('singing', 'reading') with an infinitive ('to dance'). Correct: 'She likes singing, dancing and reading.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Identify the error type: 'The cost of the books are high.'
questions.explanation: The real subject is 'cost' (singular), not 'books'. Correct: 'The cost of the books is high.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Identify the error type: 'My brother is taller than me in height.'
questions.explanation: 'In height' is redundant with 'taller'. Correct: 'My brother is taller than I am.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Identify the error type: 'The climate of Mysuru is cooler than Bengaluru.'
questions.explanation: It compares 'climate' with 'Bengaluru' (a city), which are unlike things. Correct: 'The climate of Mysuru is cooler than that of Bengaluru.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.

options.A: Because it was raining. We stayed home.
options.B: Because it was raining, we stayed home.
options.C: Because it was raining; we stayed home.
options.D: Because it was raining we stayed home.

questions.explanation: A fragment is corrected by joining the dependent clause to the main clause with a comma.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.

options.A: I was tired, I went to bed.
options.B: I was tired, so I went to bed.
options.C: I was tired I went to bed.
options.D: I was tired; so, I went to bed.

questions.explanation: A comma splice is corrected by adding a coordinator ('so') after the comma.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.

options.A: Walking to school, the rain started.
options.B: While I was walking to school, it started raining.
options.C: Walking to school, it started raining.

questions.explanation: A dangling modifier is corrected by supplying the logical subject ('I') for the modifying phrase.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.

options.A: She likes singing, to dance and reading.
options.B: She likes singing, dancing and reading.
